title: X-ray polarization in magnetized neutron stars
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures
summary: X-ray polarimetry has opened a new window into understanding the physics around magnetized compact objects. IXPE detection of linear polarization from such systems has prompted a new spurt of theoretical modeling. Our study is based on the dominant paradigm that the observed polarization arises from the scattering of photons around highly magnetized systems. Our main focus is the dependence of the polarization of the scattered light on properties of the incoming light, i.e., geometry and the polarization state, and the determination of the spectral shape of the polarized light for a wide range of magnetic field strengths. We also analyze the impact of vacuum birefringence on photon polarization. We show that, generically, we expect a higher linear degree of polarization from magnetars as compared to normal pulsars, which is in agreement with IXPE observations. Under some conditions, our study helps to understand the observed degree of polarization from normal pulsars and low-magnetized neutron stars and their spectral dependence. However, we cannot conclusively explain the spectral shape of the observed polarization for magnetars using only a single component emission from scattering in a strong magnetic field. This probably points to the system being more complex, e.g., multi-component, than our study allows for. Upcoming X-ray polarimeters with broader energy coverage could probe some of our other predictions, e.g., the spectral shape of the polarized light close to the resonance frequency.

AI.tldr: This paper models X-ray polarization from scattering in strong magnetic fields, showing magnetars should have higher linear polarization than normal pulsars (matching IXPE data), but a single scattering component cannot fully explain magnetar polarization spectra, suggesting multi-component emission.
AI.motivation: To understand the physics around magnetized compact objects (magnetars, pulsars) using the new window of X-ray polarimetry opened by IXPE, and to model how photon scattering in strong magnetic fields produces observed polarization signals.
AI.method: Theoretical modeling of scattering of photons in highly magnetized systems, analyzing dependence of polarization on incoming light geometry and polarization state, determining spectral shape across a wide range of magnetic field strengths, and incorporating vacuum birefringence effects on photon polarization.
AI.result: Magnetars generically show higher linear degree of polarization than normal pulsars (consistent with IXPE). The model helps explain polarization from normal pulsars and low-magnetized neutron stars but cannot fully explain magnetar polarization spectral shape with a single scattering component.
AI.conclusion: A single-component scattering model is insufficient for magnetars, pointing to more complex (multi-component) emission. Future X-ray polarimeters with broader energy coverage could test predictions such as spectral shape near the resonance frequency.

title: Constraining the near-source relativistic wind medium using Fast Radio Burst circular polarization data
comment: Comments encouraged. 21 pages, 10 figures, 1 table. Submitted for review
summary: Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) exhibit diverse spectro-temporal characteristics, which can probe vital propagation and source physics via Stokes polarimetry. We investigate whether the circular polarization (Stokes $V$) observed in some bursts is produced by Faraday conversion in the near-source wind of magnetars rather than being intrinsic to the source. Our calculation includes the increase in the effective mass of $e^\pm$ in the presence of the FRB wave. We find that Faraday conversion in the magnetar wind can explain the broad range of observed circular polarization in FRBs, including its frequent non-detection. Observationally derived upper limits on $V$ provide stringent constraints on the wind luminosity, magnetization, bulk Lorentz factor, and effective particle mass when ions are present. When available, frequency resolved Stokes spectra offer direct estimates of the wind environment. The Stokes parameters can undergo rapid oscillations with frequency in the high-wind/low-FRB-luminosity regime, resulting in Stokes-V depolarization. Bursts with significantly lower luminosities than typical FRBs can also develop measurable circular polarization, within the model framework. Additionally, separate zones are favored for significant circular polarization and rotation measure, when the model is applicable. The model constrains instantaneous wind parameters for several sources, including FRB 20201124A, FRB 20180301A, and SGR 1935+2154. This work represents the first instance in which properties of winds from compact objects associated with FRBs are inferred from polarization data.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether circular polarization in Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) originates from Faraday conversion in magnetar winds rather than being intrinsic, finding the model can explain observed polarization diversity and constrain wind properties for several sources.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the circular polarization observed in some FRBs is produced by Faraday conversion in near-source magnetar winds, which would provide a probe of propagation and source physics.
AI.method: The authors calculate Faraday conversion in magnetar winds, including the effective mass increase of e± pairs due to the FRB wave, and compare model predictions with observed Stokes V data and upper limits.
AI.result: Faraday conversion in magnetar winds can explain the broad range of observed circular polarization and its frequent non-detection. Upper limits on V constrain wind luminosity, magnetization, bulk Lorentz factor, and effective particle mass. Stokes parameters can oscillate rapidly with frequency, causing depolarization in high-wind/low-luminosity regimes. Separate zones are favored for significant circular polarization and rotation measure.
AI.conclusion: This is the first instance where wind properties of compact objects associated with FRBs are inferred from polarization data, constraining instantaneous wind parameters for FRB 20201124A, FRB 20180301A, and SGR 1935+2154.

title: Extreme outflow velocities and weak UV emission lines indicate quasars shedding their dust cocoons
comment: 30 pages, 27 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: The recently discovered low-ionisation broad absorption line (LoBAL) quasar GQ 1309$+$2904 is unusual due to its very broad, highly blueshifted absorption troughs and an absence of broad emission lines except for ${\mathrm{H} α}$. In this paper, we present observations of six quasars that appear very similar to GQ 1309$+$2904 in the rest-frame ultraviolet (UV). We measure the systemic redshifts of these quasars to be $z\approx$ 2.07--3.28 from detected ${\mathrm{H} α}$ emission lines. We confirm that all targets are quasars with highly blueshifted BALs possessing high-speed outflows with velocities up to $\sim 0.16\,c$, and five of them are confidently identified as LoBAL quasars. Based on ${\mathrm{H} α}$ emission, black hole masses and Eddington ratios of these quasars are $M_{\mathrm{BH}} \approx 10^{8.7}$--$10^{9.4}\,M_{\odot}$ and $L_{\mathrm{bol}} / L_{\mathrm{Edd}} \approx$ 0.14--0.34, indicating that their central black holes are very massive and active. Every quasar in our sample exhibits a very flat or reddened continuum. The spectral shapes of three objects are well-fitted by a normal quasar composite reddened by a Small-Magellanic-Cloud-like (SMC-like) extinction curve, while the other three require a steeper extinction law. Broad-band ($BVR$) polarimetry for two of the latter group (plus GQ 1309$+$2904) reveals their low polarisations, consistent with low inclination (more face-on) angles. We propose that these objects are weak emission-line quasars (WLQs) observed through the disc wind, caught emerging from their dust cocoons. As quasars shed their cocoons, dust grains in the disc wind are shattered into smaller particles, producing the UV-steeper extinction curve observed along the outflow. We present a schematic illustration of this shedding process that can account for the peculiar spectral features observed in our sample.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies six quasars similar to the unusual LoBAL quasar GQ 1309+2904, with highly blueshifted broad absorption lines, high-speed outflows up to 0.16c, massive black holes (10^8.7–10^9.4 M⊙), Eddington ratios of 0.14–0.34, and reddened continua. Polarimetry suggests low inclinations, and the authors propose these are weak emission-line quasars observed through disc winds emerging from dust cocoons, where dust shattering produces steep UV extinction.
AI.motivation: To understand the nature of quasars with very broad, highly blueshifted absorption troughs and weak broad emission lines, and to investigate whether they represent an evolutionary phase where quasars emerge from dust cocoons.
AI.method: Optical and near-infrared spectroscopy to measure systemic redshifts via Hα emission, UV spectral analysis, SED fitting with SMC-like and steeper extinction laws, broad-band BVR polarimetry, and black hole mass estimation from Hα line widths and luminosities.
AI.result: All six are quasars with high-speed BAL outflows up to 0.16c; five are confirmed LoBAL quasars; black hole masses are ~10^8.7–10^9.4 M⊙; Eddington ratios are 0.14–0.34; continua are flat or reddened; three objects fit SMC-like extinction while three need steeper extinction; polarimetry shows low polarization consistent with low inclination.
AI.conclusion: These objects are weak emission-line quasars viewed through disc winds during a dust-shedding evolutionary phase. Dust grain shattering in the outflow produces the steeper UV extinction, and a schematic model of this shedding process explains the observed spectral peculiarities.

title: AI-enabled gravitational-waves searches for binary neutron stars at optimal sensitivity
summary: Gravitational Waves (GWs) represent the newest window of astronomy, furthering our understanding of compact objects like black holes and neutron stars in the Universe. The signal from two merging neutron stars is especially interesting since it brings the prospect of concordant electromagnetic and neutrino emissions. Such multi-messenger observations have a transformational impact on fundamental physics, nuclear matter, astrophysics, and gravity. It was first witnessed in 2017 with the detection of the binary neutron star (BNS) merger GW170817. However, searching for BNS signals in real-time in the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) GW detectors presents a computational challenge, as the data streaming out must be matched against $\sim$ million reference waveforms, which requires up to a thousand CPU cores. We present a different approach using neural networks to learn the presence of a signal in the data. Our algorithm, called Aframe, was deployed in the LVK's fourth observing run and was the first artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled search to detect multiple binary black holes (BBHs) live. In this work, we demonstrate that the approach extends to the lower-mass BNS regime, and is the first AI-enabled search that achieves sensitivity comparable to matched-filter pipelines at lower computational and latency costs. The challenge of the longer-duration BNS signals is addressed by heterodyning the data, following which the network architecture used for BBHs is sufficient to distinguish signal versus background. We also show that this analysis requires a single non-flagship GPU for online deployment. Furthermore, the design and adoption of inference-as-a-service tools allow rapid offline analysis using a distributed pool of GPU resources. Hence, aside from the use case of rapid online data analysis, we also establish the use of Aframe for efficient archival data analysis.

AI.tldr: Aframe is a neural network-based gravitational wave search that, for the first time, achieves sensitivity comparable to matched-filter pipelines for binary neutron star mergers at lower computational cost, using heterodyning to handle longer-duration signals, and can be deployed on a single non-flagship GPU for online analysis or distributed GPU resources for offline archival analysis.
AI.motivation: Real-time searching for binary neutron star (BNS) signals in LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA data is computationally challenging, requiring matching streaming data against ~million reference waveforms and up to a thousand CPU cores; existing matched-filter pipelines are computationally expensive.
AI.method: The authors present Aframe, a neural network-based algorithm that learns the presence of GW signals in data. For longer-duration BNS signals, they use heterodyning (downmixing) to reduce the data rate, then apply the same network architecture previously used for binary black holes (BBHs). The system was deployed using inference-as-a-service tools for both online (single GPU) and offline (distributed GPU pool) analysis.
AI.result: Aframe achieved sensitivity comparable to matched-filter pipelines for BNS signals with lower computational and latency costs. It was deployed in LVK's fourth observing run, was the first AI-enabled search to detect multiple BBHs live, and now extends to the BNS regime. The analysis requires only a single non-flagship GPU for online deployment.
AI.conclusion: Neural networks can effectively replace computationally expensive matched-filtering for BNS detection at lower cost, and the inference-as-a-service design enables both rapid online analysis and efficient archival data analysis.

title: The fingerprint of primordial mass segregation on the tidal tails of star clusters
summary: We investigate the effect of primordial mass segregation (PMS) in shaping the tidal tail structures of star clusters, searching for any trace of PMS on the tails at both early and late evolutionary stages. Through N-body simulations, we analyze clusters with two different degrees of PMS at various Galactocentric distances (R_G), considering two black hole retention scenarios. Our findings reveal that PMS influences early cluster expansion and the formation of tidal tails with a bottom-heavy stellar mass function, this being more pronounced at smaller R_G but diminishes over time. Primordially segregated clusters exhibit denser, unified, and longer tail structures compared to non-segregated clusters. The mean stellar mass distribution along the tails shows distinct patterns for primordially segregated and non-segregated clusters, converging at later evolutionary stages. The retention of stellar remnants has a weak impact on the mean mass distribution along the tails and on its morphology. We find that although mean mass differences persist along the tidal tails, the rate of change in primordially mass-segregated clusters eventually converges with that of non-segregated clusters, suggesting that the influence of primordial mass segregation on the tidal tails gradually diminishes over the course of cluster evolution.

AI.tldr: This study uses N-body simulations to investigate how primordial mass segregation (PMS) affects tidal tail structures of star clusters. PMS leads to denser, longer tidal tails with bottom-heavy stellar mass functions early on, especially at smaller Galactocentric distances, but these effects diminish over time as segregated and non-segregated clusters converge.
AI.motivation: To understand whether primordial mass segregation leaves detectable traces on the tidal tails of star clusters across different evolutionary stages and Galactic environments.
AI.method: N-body simulations of star clusters with two degrees of PMS at varying Galactocentric distances, considering two black hole retention scenarios.
AI.result: PMS causes early cluster expansion and bottom-heavy tidal tails (stronger at smaller R_G); primordially segregated clusters have denser, longer, more unified tails; mean mass distributions differ initially but converge later; black hole retention has weak effects on tail morphology and mass distribution.
AI.conclusion: Primordial mass segregation influences tidal tail properties at early stages, but its signature diminishes over time as segregated and non-segregated clusters converge in their evolutionary paths.

title: Magneto-rotational instabilities in solids: application to neutron-star crusts
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures. Accepted for publication in Phys. Rev. D
summary: The magneto-rotational instability can generate strong, turbulent substructure within magnetised shear flows. The efficacy of the mechanism as a function of microphysical aspects of the fluid, such as stratification and diffusivity, has been explored extensively. One aspect that has not been studied thus far, however, is whether the instability can also operate in solids. Motivated by the possibility that solid regions within planets or degenerate stars may rotate differentially with respect to liquid or gaseous layers during some phase of their life, we examine the extent to which elasticity suppresses the instability. A simplified, plane-parallel analysis reveals that only in cases where the flow is strongly sheared, such that the magnetic tension that would result from the instability in a liquid exceeds the shear modulus of the elastic cavity, can magnetic growth occur. In the context of dynamical tides in binary neutron-star mergers, this implies that the magnetic field can be amplified in the crust prior to coalescence only if the star boasts a spin frequency of $\gtrsim 300$Hz. If viscous heating weakens the crystalline structure prior to resonance, the required spin frequency is reduced.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether the magneto-rotational instability (MRI) can operate in solid elastic media, such as planetary or stellar crusts. Using a plane-parallel analysis, the authors find that MRI is only possible if the magnetic tension from the instability exceeds the shear modulus of the solid—requiring sufficiently strong shear flows. In binary neutron-star mergers, this implies magnetic field amplification in the crust requires a spin frequency ≳300 Hz, though viscous heating can lower this threshold.
AI.motivation: The magneto-rotational instability (MRI) is well-studied in fluids (with stratification and diffusivity), but whether it can also operate in solid regions (e.g., within planets or degenerate stars) has not been explored. This gap motivates the study, particularly given that solid layers may rotate differentially relative to liquid/gaseous layers during certain evolutionary phases.
AI.method: The authors employ a simplified, plane-parallel analysis to examine the conditions under which elasticity suppresses the MRI. They compare the magnetic tension generated by the instability (as it would operate in a liquid) against the shear modulus of the solid elastic cavity to determine the threshold for magnetic growth.
AI.result: MRI can operate in solids only when the flow is strongly sheared such that the magnetic tension exceeds the shear modulus of the elastic medium. Applied to binary neutron-star mergers, crustal magnetic field amplification prior to coalescence requires a spin frequency ≳300 Hz. If viscous heating weakens the crystalline structure, the required spin frequency decreases.
AI.conclusion: Elasticity suppresses the magneto-rotational instability except under strongly sheared conditions where magnetic tension overcomes the shear modulus. This sets a spin-frequency threshold for MRI-driven magnetic amplification in neutron-star crusts, with potential lowering via viscous pre-resonance heating.

title: IRIS: Deciphering Spectral-Line Imagery of the Galactic Center by Machine-Learning on Simulations
summary:
In understanding the 3D structure of the Milky Way's Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), we are limited by our edge-on perspective. Towards addressing this problem, we introduce Imagery Reversion Informed by Simulation (IRIS). IRIS is a novel machine-learning code base featuring a deep convolutional neural network (CNN), which we have designed to translate edge-on observations of our Milky Way Galaxy into top-down images by training on data generated from AREPO galaxy simulations and synthetic observations of those simulations.
  We develop a large custom dataset on which we train our bespoke model, and then test the trained model on synthetic data to probe the potential of this machine-learning method, which we call supervised reversion. We then apply our trained model to real observations from the SEDIGISM 13CO(2-1) survey, yielding new top-down views of our CMZ. Though our SEDIGISM reversions are not fully consistent across model training runs, we posit that this lack of convergence can be alleviated by expansion of the training dataset. We argue that these results represent a strong proof-of-concept for the use of supervised reversion to decipher our CMZ's 3D structure.
  Crucial in generating our training dataset's 100k synthetic observations, we introduce IRIS Synthetic Observation (IRIS-SO), a new GPU-accelerated and fully differentiable code implemented in PyTorch for the non-LTE synthetic observation of spectral lines and dust. We find that IRIS-SO provides up to 10,000x speedups in comparison to the synthetic-observation code RADMC-3D. We release all the IRIS code open-source at https://github.com/bldubois/IRIS.

AI.tldr: IRIS is a CNN-based machine learning framework that translates edge-on molecular line observations of the Milky Way's Central Molecular Zone into top-down views. It uses AREPO simulations to generate training data, introduces the GPU-accelerated IRIS-SO synthetic observation code (up to 10,000× faster than RADMC-3D), and demonstrates proof-of-concept via reversions of SEDIGISM 13CO(2-1) data.
AI.motivation: We are limited by our edge-on perspective in understanding the 3D structure of the Milky Way's Central Molecular Zone (CMZ).
AI.method: IRIS uses a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on synthetic data generated from AREPO galaxy simulations and synthetic observations, then applies the trained model to real SEDIGISM 13CO(2-1) observations to produce top-down views. The IRIS-SO code provides GPU-accelerated non-LTE synthetic observations of spectral lines and dust in PyTorch.
AI.result: The model yields new top-down views of the CMZ from SEDIGISM data, though reversions are not fully consistent across training runs. IRIS-SO provides up to 10,000× speedups over RADMC-3D.
AI.conclusion: The results represent a strong proof-of-concept for using supervised reversion to decipher the CMZ's 3D structure. Lack of convergence can be alleviated by expanding the training dataset.

title: Signatures of Two Distinct Epochs of FRB 20240114A from January to August 2024 Based on its Energy and Waiting Time Analysis
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: A comprehensive analysis of the energy and waiting time distributions of the bursts from FRB 20240114A detected by the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope between 28 January and 29 August 2024 is presented. For the full sample, its energy distribution cannot be fitted with the simple power-law (SPL),bent power-law (BPL), thresholded power-law (TPL) or Band function models, and its waiting time distribution excluding intervals shorter than 0.5 s cannot be fitted with the Poisson or Weibull models. Nevertheless, for the subsamples with more than 50 bursts in single-day observations, their energy distributions can be fitted with the BPL or TPL models, and their waiting time distributions are better described by a Weibull model. It is noted that the best-fitting BPL parameter $β$ is approximately invariant within the epochs before and after 21 March 2024, with an average of $\bar β_b = 1.006 \pm 0.074$ and $\bar β_a = 1.236 \pm 0.183$ (one standard deviation), respectively. Most subsamples from the later epoch have a smaller burst rate parameter $r$ in the Weibull model than those from the earlier epoch. The majority of bursts with $E>10^{39}$ erg occurred in the earlier epoch. The energy distributions in the high-energy range ($> 6\times10^{37}$ erg) differ significantly between the two epochs, and power-law fits to $dN/dE$ yield indices of $-1.97_{-0.02}^{+0.02}$ and $-2.34_{-0.06}^{+0.06}$, respectively. The median of the waiting time distribution of the later epoch is larger than that in the earlier epoch. These results suggest that the two epochs may be dominated by different types of bursts, possibly attributed to changes in the physical properties of the emission region.

AI.tldr: Analysis of FRB 20240114A bursts detected by FAST (Jan–Aug 2024) shows that full-sample energy/waiting time distributions cannot be fitted by standard models, but daily subsamples with >50 bursts fit BPL/TPL and Weibull models. Two distinct epochs (before/after March 21, 2024) exhibit different burst properties: invariant BPL β parameters within epochs, different burst rates, high-energy power-law indices (-1.97 vs -2.34), and larger waiting times in the later epoch, suggesting different burst types due to changes in the emission region's physical properties.
AI.motivation: To characterize the energy and waiting time distributions of FRB 20240114A bursts detected by FAST over 8 months, and to identify whether distinct burst populations or epochs exist that could reveal changes in the physical properties of the emission region.
AI.method: Statistical analysis of energy distributions fitted with SPL, BPL, TPL, and Band function models; waiting time distributions fitted with Poisson and Weibull models; epoch-split analysis before and after March 21, 2024; power-law fitting of high-energy tail.
AI.result: Full-sample distributions cannot be fitted by standard models. Daily subsamples with >50 bursts fit BPL/TPL and Weibull. BPL β is invariant within epochs (β̄_b=1.006±0.074, β̄_a=1.236±0.183). Later epoch has smaller Weibull burst rate r and larger median waiting time. High-energy power-law indices: -1.97 (earlier) vs -2.34 (later). Most >10^39 erg bursts occurred in the earlier epoch.
AI.conclusion: The two epochs may be dominated by different types of bursts, possibly due to changes in the physical properties of the emission region of FRB 20240114A.

title: Fractional-Dimension Gravity and the Milky Way Galaxy
comment: 19 pages, including 6 figures. Eight paper on Fractional-Dimension Gravity
summary:
In this work, we focus our analysis of Fractional-Dimension Gravity (FDG) on our home galaxy, the Milky Way (MW), by using the latest Gaia DR3 data as well as previous rotation curve (RC) data for this galaxy. FDG is an alternative gravitational model (previously known as Newtonian Fractional-Dimension Gravity - NFDG) which does not require the dark matter (DM) paradigm.
  The MW is studied here with the methods of FDG and its observed rotation curves are successfully reproduced by using a variable fractional dimension $D\left (R\right)$, following previous studies of several other galaxies which were analyzed with the same methodology. An alternative dimension function $D_{m}\left(R \right)$, based on the mass-dimension field equation, was also used and yielded less accurate fits to the experimental data.
  In addition, we also considered possible implications of the FDG metric, based on the presence of additional weights, on the structure of Special Relativity (SR) for spacetimes with fractional dimension. One notable outcome of this analysis is the possibility of an effective superluminal motion in galactic regions where the space dimension is $D<3$. Although this result is very speculative, it opens interesting new perspectives for possible interstellar travel in our galaxy.

AI.tldr: This paper tests Fractional-Dimension Gravity (FDG) on Milky Way rotation curve data (Gaia DR3), finding successful fits using a variable fractional dimension, and speculates on superluminal motion possibilities in regions where spatial dimension D < 3.
AI.motivation: To test FDG as an alternative to dark matter for explaining the Milky Way's rotation curve, and to explore speculative implications of FDG metric for Special Relativity and superluminal motion.
AI.method: FDG applied to Milky Way rotation curves using Gaia DR3 and previous RC data; compared two dimension functions: variable D(R) and mass-dimension-based D_m(R). Also analyzed FDG metric implications for SR in fractional-dimension spacetimes.
AI.result: Variable fractional dimension D(R) successfully reproduces MW rotation curves; D_m(R) yields less accurate fits. Speculative result: effective superluminal motion possible where spatial dimension D < 3.
AI.conclusion: FDG works well for the Milky Way without dark matter, and although speculative, the possibility of superluminal motion in D<3 regions opens interesting perspectives for interstellar travel.

title: Bolometric correction factor and radiative efficiency for the super-Eddington accretion flow in tidal disruption events
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: The estimate of the bolometric luminosity and the radiative efficiency are two key aspects for understanding the properties of the accretion flow around a supermassive black hole (BH). In this paper, we focus on the estimate of the bolometric luminosity and the radiative efficiency of the early super-Eddington accretion flow in tidal disruption events (TDEs). Specifically, we first perform radiation hydrodynamic simulations of super-Eddington accretion flow in TDE environment, and then calculate the corresponding emergent spectra with the method of post processing for the simulation data. Based on the emergent spectra, we calculate the isotropic-equivalent X-ray bolometric correction factor $k_\mathrm{bol}$ and the radiative efficiency $η$ of the super-Eddington accretion flow. We find that both $k_\mathrm{bol}$ and $η$ are BH mass and viewing-angle dependent. $k_\mathrm{bol}$ is in the range of about a few tens to a few thousands, and $η$ is in the range of $\sim 10^{-3}-10^{-1}$ for BH mass in the range of $10^{6-7}M_\odot$ and the viewing angle in the range of $0^{\rm o}-90^{\rm o}$. Finally, we apply the derived $k_\mathrm{bol}$ and $η$ to some specific TDEs to estimate the accreted mass during an event, which can significantly alleviate the so-called missing energy problem in TDEs.

AI.tldr: This paper uses radiation hydrodynamic simulations and post-processing to calculate bolometric correction factors (k_bol ~ tens to thousands) and radiative efficiencies (η ~ 10⁻³–10⁻¹) for super-Eddington accretion flows in TDEs, finding both are BH mass and viewing-angle dependent, and applying them to TDEs to alleviate the missing energy problem.
AI.motivation: To improve estimates of bolometric luminosity and radiative efficiency in super-Eddington accretion flows during tidal disruption events, addressing uncertainties in these key parameters for understanding accretion flow properties around supermassive black holes.
AI.method: Performed radiation hydrodynamic simulations of super-Eddington accretion flow in TDE environments, followed by post-processing to calculate emergent spectra, from which isotropic-equivalent X-ray bolometric correction factor k_bol and radiative efficiency η were derived.
AI.result: k_bol ranges from ~tens to thousands, η ranges ~10⁻³–10⁻¹, and both depend on BH mass (10⁶–10⁷ M⊙) and viewing angle (0°–90°). Application to specific TDEs alleviates the missing energy problem.
AI.conclusion: The derived k_bol and η enable better estimation of accreted mass in TDEs, significantly mitigating the missing energy problem in these events.

title: Radiative filtering unifies broad-line phenomenology in active galactic nuclei
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, as Letter to Astrophysical Journal
summary: Broad emission lines (BELs) are a defining feature of active galactic nuclei (AGNs), yet they weaken or disappear in both very low- and very high-accretion systems. These regimes are typically treated separately, and a unified physical explanation has remained elusive. Here we show that this behavior arises if line formation is governed not by the intrinsic luminosity of the central engine, but by the ionizing radiation field that survives filtering before reaching the broad-line region (BLR). In this picture, line production depends on the product of intrinsic ionizing capability and an effective transmission. Because the former increases from low accretion rates while the latter declines at high accretion rates, the effective ionizing field naturally develops a finite and non-universal window for BEL formation. This framework unifies the absence or extreme faintness of BELs in low-luminosity AGNs, LINERs, and weak-line quasars (WLQs), and accounts for the Baldwin effect and the $R_{\rm Fe}$ trend. It also necessarily implies the breakdown of standard BLR-based scaling relations in extreme accretion regimes. We show that a minimal quantitative realization reproduces this behavior across black-hole mass, accretion rate, and radiative efficiency. These results suggest that AGN emission-line phenomenology is governed by global regulation of the ionizing radiation field rather than by mere presence or condition of local gas.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that broad emission line (BEL) strength in AGNs depends not on central engine luminosity alone, but on the ionizing radiation field after filtering. This unifies BEL disappearance in both low- and high-accretion regimes, explains the Baldwin effect and R_Fe trends, and implies breakdown of standard BLR scaling relations in extreme accretion regimes.
AI.motivation: BELs weaken or disappear in both very low- and very high-accretion AGN systems, yet these regimes are typically treated separately with no unified physical explanation.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework where BEL formation depends on the product of intrinsic ionizing capability and effective transmission. A minimal quantitative realization is tested across black-hole mass, accretion rate, and radiative efficiency.
AI.result: The model produces a finite, non-universal window for BEL formation, unifying BEL absence/faintness in low-luminosity AGNs, LINERs, and WLQs, and accounting for the Baldwin effect and R_Fe trend.
AI.conclusion: AGN emission-line phenomenology is governed by global regulation of the ionizing radiation field rather than merely local gas conditions, implying breakdown of standard BLR scaling relations in extreme accretion regimes.

title: X-ray Fourier lag-frequency spectra modulated by stochastic turbulent acceleration in the jets of high-frequency-peaked BL Lac
comment: 17 pages, 10 figures, published in PRD
summary: X-ray interband time lags are key diagnostics of jet physics and are frequently detected in high-frequency peaked BL Lac (HBL) objects at different epochs with various X-ray telescopes. In this work, we theoretically investigate Fourier lag-frequency spectra using a generic one-zone leptonic model incorporating the stochastic turbulent acceleration (STA), which plays a crucial role in shaping the emitted photon spectra. We demonstrate that the competition between STA, radiative cooling, and escape processes not only gives rise to two well-defined time-lag regimes: hard/positive and soft/negative lags, but also reveals the existence of a transition between the two regimes. Our results indicate that time lags in the transitional and soft-lag regimes can be clearly amplified and modified by STA's suppression of high-energy electron cooling, and nonlinear synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) cooling can further amplify the emergence of time lags. We conclude that the adopted model offers a unifying quantitative framework for interpreting the diverse time-lag signatures observed in the X-ray flares of HBLs. Additionally, SSC cooling effects can account for the relatively large lags observed in TeV-bright flares, as well as the observed trend between lag amplitude and flare duration: the larger the flare duration, the larger the lag.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a one-zone leptonic model with stochastic turbulent acceleration (STA) to theoretically investigate X-ray interband time lags in HBL objects, finding that STA, radiative cooling, and escape produce hard/positive, soft/negative, and transitional lag regimes, with SSC cooling amplifying lags and explaining observed trends like the correlation between lag amplitude and flare duration.
AI.motivation: X-ray interband time lags are key diagnostics of jet physics in HBL objects, yet a unified theoretical framework explaining the diverse lag signatures observed across different epochs and telescopes has been lacking.
AI.method: A generic one-zone leptonic model incorporating stochastic turbulent acceleration (STA) is used to theoretically compute Fourier lag-frequency spectra, analyzing the competition between STA, radiative cooling, and electron escape processes.
AI.result: The model produces two well-defined lag regimes (hard/positive and soft/negative) plus a transitional regime. STA suppresses high-energy electron cooling, amplifying lags in transitional and soft-lag regimes. Nonlinear SSC cooling further amplifies time lags and accounts for large lags in TeV-bright flares and the positive correlation between lag amplitude and flare duration.
AI.conclusion: The one-zone leptonic STA model provides a unifying quantitative framework for interpreting diverse X-ray time-lag signatures in HBL flares, with SSC cooling explaining the observed lag-duration trend and large lags in TeV-bright events.

title: The Galactic Centre G+0.633-0.0604 molecular cloud: a new astrochemical gold mine. I. Gas physical properties
comment: 20 pages, 11 figures, 8 tables, 6 appendix - Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: In the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), shocks play a key role in triggering star formation and driving chemical enrichment. The Sgr B2 complex is a prime template, hosting massive protoclusters (N, M, S) and the northern G+0.693 cloud, which exhibits shock-induced prestellar signatures. We report on G+0.633-0.0604, a newly identified shock-dominated and chemically rich cloud at the southern edge of Sgr B2, where the next star formation episodes are proposed. We characterise its physical properties and the shocks shaping it. We present analyses on CH$_3$CCH, CH$_3$CN, HC$_3$N, HNCO and several isotopologues of CO to infer the gas $T_{\rm kin}$ and density, using high-sensitivity spectral surveys from the Yebes 40m, IRAM 30m and APEX radio telescopes that covered ~100 GHz across the 31-275 GHz range. We also used 3 mm IRAM 30m mosaics (13'$\times$13') of Sgr B2 in HC$_3$N, HNCO and C$_2$H$_5$OH to probe G+0.633 environment. We identify three velocity components: a narrow main one (C1, $v_{\rm LSR}$~48.5 km/s; FWHM~10 km/s), and two broader, fainter components at higher velocities, C2 (~61 km/s; ~13 km/s) and C3 (~89 km/s; ~18 km/s), all showing similar properties ($T_{\rm kin}$~55-90 K, $N_{\rm H_2}$~(3-7)$\times$10$^{22}$ cm$^{-2}$, $n_{\rm H_2}$~(0.5-2.5)$\times$10$^{4}$ cm$^{-3}$) and extended distributions. C1 delineates G+0.633 physically and coincides with a peak in HNCO, supporting a shock-driven origin likely rooted in the cloud-cloud collision shaping Sgr B2 and also traced by C2, which extends north to G+0.693. C3 is kinematically unlinked and related to large-scale CMZ dynamics. Of the three, C1 may represent a very early protocluster phase, yet to be confirmed. G+0.633 thus emerges as a new shock-dominated CMZ cloud resembling G+0.693, providing another unique laboratory to investigate how shocks drive molecular complexity and regulate the onset of cluster formation in the CMZ.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies G+0.633-0.0604 as a newly discovered shock-dominated, chemically rich molecular cloud at the southern edge of Sgr B2 in the Central Molecular Zone. Using multi-telescope spectral surveys, the authors characterize three velocity components (C1, C2, C3) with similar physical properties (T_kin~55-90 K, N_H2~(3-7)×10^22 cm^-2, n_H2~(0.5-2.5)×10^4 cm^-3). C1 defines the cloud's physical structure and shows shock signatures (HNCO peak), C2 connects to the known G+0.693 cloud via cloud-cloud collision dynamics, and C3 is kinematically unrelated to Sgr B2. G+0.633 is proposed as an early protocluster phase and a new laboratory for studying shock-driven chemistry and star formation in the CMZ.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize a newly discovered shock-dominated molecular cloud (G+0.633-0.0604) at the southern edge of the Sgr B2 complex, investigating how shocks drive molecular complexity and regulate the onset of cluster formation in the Central Molecular Zone.
AI.method: High-sensitivity spectral surveys from Yebes 40m, IRAM 30m, and APEX radio telescopes covering ~100 GHz across 31-275 GHz, plus 3 mm IRAM 30m mosaics (13'×13') of Sgr B2. Analysis of CH3CCH, CH3CN, HC3N, HNCO, and CO isotopologues to infer gas kinetic temperature and density.
AI.result: Three velocity components identified: C1 (narrow main, v_LSR~48.5 km/s, FWHM~10 km/s), C2 (~61 km/s, ~13 km/s), C3 (~89 km/s, ~18 km/s). All show similar properties (T_kin~55-90 K, N_H2~(3-7)×10^22 cm^-2, n_H2~(0.5-2.5)×10^4 cm^-3) and extended distributions. C1 coincides with HNCO peak supporting shock origin from cloud-cloud collision; C2 extends north to G+0.693; C3 relates to large-scale CMZ dynamics.
AI.conclusion: G+0.633-0.0604 is a newly identified shock-dominated CMZ cloud resembling G+0.693, with C1 representing a possible very early protocluster phase. It provides a unique laboratory to investigate how shocks drive molecular complexity and regulate the onset of cluster formation in the Central Molecular Zone.

title: Polarization Architecture of Steady GRMHD Jets from the Horizon to Infinity
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures
summary: We develop a semi-analytic framework for stationary, axisymmetric GRMHD jets that efficiently generates resolved polarized images from the near-horizon region out to $\sim 10^5\,r_g$ across a broad parameter space, enabling rapid exploration of how gravity and magnetohydrodynamic flows imprint scale-dependent signatures on jet morphology and polarization. We identify a new scale-dependent separation in polarimetric diagnostics. Outside the photon ring, plasma loading strongly modifies the polarization-angle profile of the integrated jet-layer emission through inertia-driven winding of the magnetic field. At large image-plane radii, the polarization angle follows a power-law in radius, with an index determined by the jet collimation profile. Near the horizon, in contrast, jets converge to a universal polarization pattern controlled solely by black hole spin. This convergence is hierarchical: differences in velocity and magnetic-field structure are erased first, whereas collimation-dependent differences persist to smaller radii, thereby allowing these effects to be disentangled. These results establish a largely achromatic polarimetric diagnostic that connects GRMHD jet dynamics to resolved image structure, with direct implications for high-resolution polarimetry and for constraining black hole spin and jet formation.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a semi-analytic framework for GRMHD jets that produces polarized images from near-horizon to large scales, revealing a scale-dependent separation in polarization diagnostics: outer regions show plasma-loading-driven polarization-angle winding, while inner regions converge to a universal spin-controlled pattern, enabling disentanglement of jet dynamics and black hole properties.
AI.motivation: To enable rapid exploration of how gravity and magnetohydrodynamic flows imprint scale-dependent signatures on jet morphology and polarization across a broad parameter space, from the near-horizon region out to ~10^5 r_g.
AI.method: A semi-analytic framework for stationary, axisymmetric GRMHD jets that efficiently generates resolved polarized images across a broad parameter space.
AI.result: Identified a scale-dependent separation in polarimetric diagnostics: outside the photon ring, plasma loading modifies the polarization-angle profile via inertia-driven magnetic field winding; at large radii, the polarization angle follows a power law with an index set by the jet collimation profile; near the horizon, jets converge to a universal polarization pattern controlled solely by black hole spin, with hierarchical erasure of different physical effects.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a largely achromatic polarimetric diagnostic connecting GRMHD jet dynamics to resolved image structure, with direct implications for high-resolution polarimetry and constraining black hole spin and jet formation.

title: Post-starburst Galaxies with Active Galactic Nucleus: Properties and Evolutionary Sequences
comment: 25 pages, 12 figures. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Post-starburst (PSB) galaxies, identified by strong Balmer absorption and weak nebular emission, provide a key laboratory for studying rapid quenching. Using the final data release of the SDSS-IV MaNGA survey, we follow the traditional PSB selection criteria of Chen et al. (2019) and develop a new method to identify regions that simultaneously exhibit PSB features and nuclear activities (AGN-PSBs). Our final sample comprises 48 AGN-PSBs, 92 central PSBs (CPSBs), 89 ring-like PSBs (RPSBs), and 828 irregular PSBs (IPSBs). We find the global and spatially resolved properties of CPSBs and RPSBs are consistent with the results of Chen et al. (2019). In this work, we focus on the properties of AGN-PSBs, comparing them with CPSBs, RPSBs, and control galaxies. Similar to CPSBs and RPSBs, AGN-PSBs show positive $\mathrm{D}_{n}4000$ gradients relative to negative $\mathrm{D}_{n}4000$ gradients of their controls, which indicates younger stellar populations in the central region than that in the outskirt. Among the three sub-types, high-mass CPSBs (H-CPSBs, with $\log(M_{*}/M_{\odot})>9.5$) display the highest incidence of merger remnants and gas--star kinematic misalignment, consistent with a merger/interaction-dominated origin. AGN-PSBs and RPSBs, however, show lower and comparable fractions of merger remnants and gas--star kinematic misalignment, favoring less violent external mechanisms. Based on radial profiles of mass-weighted age and $V_{\rm star}/σ_{\rm star}$, we suggest that RPSBs can evolve into AGN-PSBs, whereas H-CPSBs likely follow a distinct evolutionary pathway. The existence of RPSBs and IPSBs also indicates that AGN feedback is not a necessary condition for the formation of PSB.

AI.tldr: Using MaNGA data, this study classifies post-starburst galaxies into four subtypes (AGN-PSBs, central PSBs, ring-like PSBs, irregular PSBs) and finds that AGN-PSBs and ring-like PSBs likely follow an evolutionary pathway distinct from high-mass central PSBs, with the latter dominated by mergers/interactions while the former involve less violent mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Post-starburst (PSB) galaxies are key laboratories for studying rapid quenching, but the role of AGN activity and the diversity of quenching mechanisms across different morphological subtypes remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Using SDSS-IV MaNGA final data release, the authors apply traditional PSB selection criteria and develop a new method to identify AGN-PSB regions. They classify 48 AGN-PSBs, 92 central PSBs (CPSBs), 89 ring-like PSBs (RPSBs), and 828 irregular PSBs (IPSBs), comparing spatially resolved properties (Dn4000 gradients, mass-weighted age, V/σ, merger remnants, kinematic misalignment) with control galaxies.
AI.result: AGN-PSBs show positive Dn4000 gradients (younger centers vs. outskirts) similar to CPSBs and RPSBs. High-mass CPSBs exhibit highest merger remnant fractions and gas-star kinematic misalignment. AGN-PSBs and RPSBs show lower merger/kinematic disturbance fractions. Radial profiles suggest RPSBs can evolve into AGN-PSBs, while high-mass CPSBs follow a distinct path.
AI.conclusion: Different PSB subtypes trace distinct quenching pathways: high-mass CPSBs are merger-dominated, while AGN-PSBs and RPSBs involve less violent external mechanisms. AGN feedback is not necessary for PSB formation, as evidenced by the existence of RPSBs and IPSBs.

title: Colour evolution in the radio afterglow of GRB 241025A
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We present the observing campaign of the afterglow of GRB241025A, a gamma-ray burst (GRB) whose prompt emission has been simultaneously detected by Swift, Einstein Probe, Fermi/GBM, SVOM, Konus-Wind and VZLUSAT-2 3U CubeSat. Our multi-wavelength campaign comprises radio, near-infrared, Optical and X-ray observations. The afterglow was clearly detected in all bands. We performed a semi-empirical fit of the data, showing that the afterglow behaviour can be reasonably reproduced by a single component, i.e. an ultra-relativistic shock. However, the results from the semi-empirical fit are inconsistent with the predicted evolution from the standard afterglow model in the slow cooling regime. Specifically, we found that at early times the synchrotron self-absorption frequency $ν_a$ should be at higher frequencies with respect to the ones sampled by our campaign, in order to explain the observed colour evolution in radio, namely the spectral evolution in time. To reconcile the prediction from the standard model with the observed data set, we fit the observations with a semi-analytical model, including a multiplicative factor $τ_{enh}$ to the optical depth which, in turn, artificially increases $ν_a$. We found that the radio colour evolution, together with the near-infrared, optical and X-ray emission, can be described reasonably well by a forward shock from a structured jet, provided that the optical depth in the shocked material is enhanced by a factor $τ_{enh}=500$. We suggest that such enhancement in the optical depth can result from a population of cold electrons in the downstream material, i.e. electrons that were not accelerated by Fermi I process at the shock front, in agreement with the theoretical expectations previously reported in the literature. Overall, our work underscores the importance of systematic, multi-frequency, multi-epoch radio follow-ups of these extreme events.

AI.tldr: Multi-wavelength (radio to X-ray) observations of GRB241025A reveal that the standard afterglow model fails to explain the radio color evolution due to an underestimated synchrotron self-absorption frequency. A structured jet model with enhanced optical depth (τ_enh=500), attributed to cold electrons not accelerated by Fermi I process, successfully reproduces the data.
AI.motivation: To understand GRB afterglow physics through a comprehensive multi-wavelength campaign (radio, NIR, optical, X-ray) of GRB241025A, which was simultaneously detected by Swift, Einstein Probe, Fermi/GBM, SVOM, Konus-Wind, and VZLUSAT-2, and to test standard afterglow model predictions against observed spectral evolution.
AI.method: Semi-empirical fitting of multi-wavelength data; semi-analytical modeling with a structured jet and an artificially enhanced optical depth factor τ_enh to raise the synchrotron self-absorption frequency ν_a.
AI.result: Standard slow-cooling model fails to match observed radio color evolution; ν_a must be higher than sampled frequencies at early times. A structured forward shock model with τ_enh=500 describes all bands well; the enhanced optical depth is interpreted as arising from cold electrons in the downstream not accelerated by Fermi I process.
AI.conclusion: Systematic multi-frequency, multi-epoch radio follow-ups are crucial for GRB afterglow studies. Cold electron populations can significantly alter the optical depth, reconciling observations with theoretical models.

title: Distance Determination of Southern Galactic Plane Supernova Remnants with the Mopra CO Survey and DECaPS 3D Dust Map
comment: 31 pages, 17 figures, accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal (AJ)
summary: Accurate distance measurements to supernova remnants (SNRs) are crucial for understanding their physical properties, evolutionary processes, and role in the Galactic interstellar medium (ISM) cycle. In this study, we apply for the first time to the southern Galactic plane a distance determination method that utilizes CO emission data from the Mopra survey to identify molecular clouds (MCs) interacting with SNRs. By combining this with extinction-distance profiles from the DECaPS three-dimensional (3D) extinction map, we directly measure the distances to the associated MCs, thereby obtaining precise distances to the remnants. To overcome the extinction-missing bias in extremely dense regions where the 3D map suffers from a deficit of background stars, we supplement our analysis with two-dimensional (2D) extinction maps as cross-validation. Applying this method, we have derived precise distances for nine SNRs: G290.1-0.8 (7.32+0.60/-0.47 kpc), G292.2-0.5 (10.85+0.43/-0.68 kpc), G296.1-0.5 (4.59+0.18/-0.19 kpc), G296.8-0.3 (8.74+0.40/-0.29 kpc), G298.6-0.0 (6.50 +/- 0.21 kpc), G312.4-0.4 (3.60+0.19/-0.23 kpc), G332.4-0.4 (2.66+0.23/-0.15 kpc), G335.2+0.1 (2.76+0.37/-0.31 kpc), and G353.6-0.7 (1.81+0.18/-0.14 kpc). Additionally, we established a robust lower distance limit of 1.34 kpc for G351.7+0.8.

AI.tldr: This study applies a novel distance determination method using CO emission data and 3D extinction maps to measure distances to nine supernova remnants in the southern Galactic plane, with cross-validation using 2D extinction maps to address biases in dense regions.
AI.motivation: Accurate distance measurements to supernova remnants are crucial for understanding their physical properties, evolutionary processes, and role in the Galactic interstellar medium cycle.
AI.method: The method uses CO emission data from the Mopra survey to identify molecular clouds interacting with SNRs, combined with extinction-distance profiles from the DECaPS 3D extinction map. For extremely dense regions with extinction-missing bias, 2D extinction maps are used as cross-validation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method successfully provides precise distance measurements for SNRs in the southern Galactic plane, with cross-validation techniques addressing limitations in dense regions.

authors: The SKA Pulsar Science Working Group
title: Testing Gravity with Binary Pulsars in the SKA Era
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/VenkatramanKrishnan01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII(AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes. An earlier version of this chapter was published in the Open Journal of Astrophysics with Arxiv ID: arXiv:2512.16161
summary: Binary (and trinary) radio pulsars are natural laboratories in space for understanding gravity in the strong field regime, with many unique and precise tests carried out so far, including the most precise tests of the strong equivalence principle and of the radiative properties of gravity. The Square Kilometre Array (SKA) telescope, with its high sensitivity in the Southern Hemisphere, will vastly improve the timing precision of recycled pulsars, allowing for a deeper search of potential deviations from general relativity (GR) in currently known systems. A Galactic census of pulsars will, in addition, will yield the discovery of dozens of relativistic pulsar systems, including potentially pulsar -- black hole binaries, which can be used to test the cosmic censorship hypothesis and the ``no-hair'' theorem. Aspects of gravitation to be explored include tests of strong equivalence principles, gravitational dipole radiation, extra field components of gravitation, gravitomagnetism, and spacetime symmetries. In this chapter, we describe the kinds of gravity tests possible with binary pulsar and outline the features and abilities that SKA must possess to best contribute to this science.

AI.tldr: The paper describes how the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) telescope will use binary and trinary radio pulsars as natural laboratories to test gravitational theories in the strong-field regime, including tests of the strong equivalence principle, gravitational radiation, the "no-hair" theorem, and cosmic censorship, by vastly improving timing precision and discovering new relativistic pulsar systems including potential pulsar-black hole binaries.
AI.motivation: Binary and trinary radio pulsars serve as natural laboratories in space for understanding gravity in the strong field regime, enabling unique and precise tests of gravitational theories including the strong equivalence principle and radiative properties of gravity.
AI.method: The SKA telescope will use its high sensitivity in the Southern Hemisphere to vastly improve timing precision of recycled pulsars, conduct a Galactic census to discover dozens of relativistic pulsar systems (including potential pulsar-black hole binaries), and perform precision timing measurements to search for deviations from general relativity.
AI.result: The SKA will enable deeper searches for deviations from GR in known systems, discovery of new relativistic pulsar systems, and tests of the cosmic censorship hypothesis, "no-hair" theorem, strong equivalence principles, gravitational dipole radiation, extra field components of gravitation, gravitomagnetism, and spacetime symmetries.
AI.conclusion: The paper outlines the kinds of gravity tests possible with binary pulsars and describes the features and abilities the SKA must possess to best contribute to strong-field gravity science.

title: Resolved HI and Environmental Dynamics
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Ramatsoku01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Spatially resolved, deep HI observations from SKA precursors and pathfinders such as MeerKAT, FAST, and ASKAP have demonstrated their ability to reveal the complex interactions between galaxies and their environments. These include, but are not limited to, recent observations of the Virgo cluster showing that the hydrodynamical effects of ram pressure stripping can operate effectively at unexpectedly large cluster-centric distances. In the Fornax cluster, the discovery of long HI tails with mixed tidal-ram-pressure origins indicates the interplay between gravitational and hydrodynamical mechanisms. Similar HI features in nearby filaments and galaxy groups, where ram pressure is expected to be weak, highlight the influence of hydrodynamical processes even in low-density environments. Multi-resolution studies have further revealed signs of cold gas accretion and HI replenishment driven by tidal interactions. While highly informative, these studies remain limited to small, specific regions of the sky. With SKA-mid AA4, it will become possible to carry out deep, spatially resolved HI imaging over hundreds of square degrees, covering environments from isolated galaxies to filaments. By reaching column-density sensitivities between $1.0 \times 10^{18}$ and $\sim 1.0 \times 10^{19}~\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$ at physical resolutions of $\sim$10 and $\sim$1 - 2 kpc, respectively, and by enabling sensitive, contiguous observations of wide areas within short integrations, SKA-mid AA4 will allow the construction of large, statistically representative samples of galaxies and detailed studies of environmental mechanisms operating across the full range of these less-studied environments at resolved scales.

AI.tldr: Current HI observations from SKA precursors reveal complex gas-dynamical interactions in galaxies (ram pressure stripping, tidal forces, cold gas accretion) but are limited to small sky regions. SKA-mid AA4 will enable deep, spatially resolved HI imaging over hundreds of square degrees at high sensitivity (~10^18-10^19 cm^-2) and resolution (~1-10 kpc), allowing statistically representative studies across diverse environments.
AI.motivation: To overcome the current limitation of HI studies to small, specific sky regions and enable statistically robust, resolved studies of environmental mechanisms (ram pressure, tidal interactions, gas accretion) across the full range of galaxy environments.
AI.method: SKA-mid AA4 will perform deep, spatially resolved HI imaging over hundreds of square degrees with column-density sensitivities of 1.0×10^18–1.0×10^19 cm^-2 at physical resolutions of ~1–2 kpc and ~10 kpc, through sensitive, contiguous wide-area observations with short integrations.
AI.result: Construction of large, statistically representative samples of galaxies and detailed, resolved-scale studies of environmental mechanisms across isolated galaxies, filaments, groups, and clusters.
AI.conclusion: SKA-mid AA4 will transform HI studies from region-specific case studies to comprehensive, statistically meaningful surveys covering the full range of galactic environments at resolved scales.

title: Timing and spectral analysis of the 2025 outburst of 4U 1630$-$47 with \textit{NICER}
comment: 13 pages, 10 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: We analyzed \textit{NICER} observations of the 2025 outburst of the black hole X-ray binary 4U~1630$-$47 to investigate the spectral--timing properties of its transient low-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) and millihertz-scale quasi-regular modulation (QRM). During the rising phase of the outburst, the QPO centroid frequency increased from $\sim 0.24$ Hz to $\sim 3.43$ Hz. Wavelet-based state separation shows that the with-QPO intervals are associated with a higher inner disk temperature and a lower \texttt{diskbb} normalization than the without-QPO intervals, while the photon index ($Γ$) shows weaker changes within the uncertainties. Near the outburst peak, the source displayed a weak QRM at $\sim 0.07$ Hz with a fractional rms amplitude of $\sim 4.7\%$, lower than that of the heartbeat state observed in 2023. Phase-resolved Hilbert--Huang analysis shows that the inner disk temperature is positively correlated with the X-ray flux, the \texttt{diskbb} normalization is anticorrelated, and $Γ$ varies only weakly. Overall, the short-timescale spectral--timing variability is expressed most clearly through the disk-related parameters. The transient QPOs are therefore consistent with short-timescale disk-related variability during the rising phase, whereas the millihertz-scale QRM may represent a weaker heartbeat-like variability mode appearing near the outburst peak.

AI.tldr: Analysis of NICER observations of the 2025 outburst of black hole X-ray binary 4U 1630–47 reveals transient low-frequency QPOs (0.24–3.43 Hz) during the rising phase, associated with higher inner disk temperature and lower diskbb normalization, and a weak millihertz-scale quasi-regular modulation (~0.07 Hz, ~4.7% rms) near the outburst peak, with disk-related parameters dominating the short-timescale spectral–timing variability.
AI.motivation: To investigate the spectral–timing properties of transient low-frequency QPOs and millihertz-scale quasi-regular modulation in the black hole X-ray binary 4U 1630–47 during its 2025 outburst, and to understand the underlying physical mechanisms.
AI.method: Wavelet-based state separation, phase-resolved Hilbert–Huang analysis of NICER observations.
AI.result: QPO centroid frequency increased from ~0.24 Hz to ~3.43 Hz during the rising phase. With-QPO intervals show higher inner disk temperature and lower diskbb normalization; Γ shows weak changes. Near outburst peak, a weak QRM at ~0.07 Hz with ~4.7% fractional rms amplitude was observed. Hilbert–Huang analysis shows inner disk temperature positively correlated with X-ray flux, diskbb normalization anticorrelated, Γ weakly varying.
AI.conclusion: Transient QPOs are consistent with short-timescale disk-related variability during the rising phase, while the millihertz-scale QRM may represent a weaker heartbeat-like variability mode near the outburst peak. Short-timescale spectral–timing variability is most clearly expressed through disk-related parameters.

title: The VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz Large Project: Polarised source counts and catalogue
comment: 13 pages, 10 figures (main text). Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: The exploration of the faint polarised radio source population is essential for interpreting the nature and evolution of magnetic fields in galaxies. While recent studies have provided insight into source counts for the $μ$Jy polarised source population at 1.4 GHz, higher frequency surveys may be more sensitive to new populations that are depolarised at lower frequencies (i.e. due to internal or external depolarisation effects). We present the deepest polarised source counts at 3 GHz to date, at an angular resolution of $1.5''$. With these relatively higher frequency observations, we aim to probe the faint polarised star-forming galaxy (SFG) population. Furthermore, through spectral modelling, we aim to provide further insight into the frequency evolution of polarised source counts. We processed the polarisation data of the VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz Large Project, one of the deepest high-resolution radio continuum surveys. We produced Stokes Q and U mosaicked channel maps. After selecting known sources in total intensity, we performed 3D rotation measure synthesis and searched for polarised emission using an empirically determined threshold. With a sensitivity of 2.6 $μ$Jy/beam in Faraday depth, we detect 65 polarised sources (51 deg$^{-2}$) above our threshold. We find that our cumulative and Euclidean-normalised source counts at 3 GHz are consistent with those in the literature at 1.4 GHz, which we attribute to the combined effect of spectral index and depolarisation in the detected sources. We detect no SFGs in our sample and derive a 2$σ$ upper limit on the density of polarised SFGs of $<2.0~\mathrm{deg}^{-2}$. This implies that significantly deeper observations will be required to readily detect this population in the SKA-era.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the deepest polarised source counts at 3 GHz (resolution 1.5″) using VLA-COSMOS data. Detecting 65 polarised sources (51 deg⁻²) at 2.6 μJy/beam sensitivity, the cumulative and Euclidean-normalised source counts are consistent with 1.4 GHz literature. No polarised star-forming galaxies (SFGs) are detected, yielding a 2σ upper limit of <2.0 deg⁻², implying deeper observations are needed for the SKA era.
AI.motivation: Understanding the faint polarised radio source population is essential for interpreting magnetic field evolution in galaxies. Higher-frequency surveys may reveal populations depolarised at lower frequencies, motivating this study at 3 GHz.
AI.method: VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz Large Project data were used to produce Stokes Q/U mosaicked channel maps. Known total-intensity sources were selected, 3D rotation measure synthesis was applied, and polarised emission was identified using an empirically determined threshold.
AI.result: 65 polarised sources (51 deg⁻²) detected above threshold at 2.6 μJy/beam sensitivity. Cumulative and Euclidean-normalised source counts at 3 GHz are consistent with 1.4 GHz literature. No SFGs detected; 2σ upper limit on polarised SFG density is <2.0 deg⁻².
AI.conclusion: The consistency between 3 GHz and 1.4 GHz source counts is attributed to combined spectral index and depolarisation effects. Significantly deeper observations will be required to detect polarised SFGs in the SKA era.

title: SN 2020bij and a Possible Slow-Rise High-Velocity Subclass of Type IIP Supernovae
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal (ApJ)
summary: Mapping how the explosion properties of Type II supernovae (SNe II) relate to the properties of their progenitors can provide strong constraints for understanding the final evolutionary stages of massive stars. Type IIP SNe, linked to the explosions of single red super-giant (RSG) stars, have recently been found to require some form of interaction with circumstellar material (CSM) to reproduce the rapid rise to the plateau often seen in their light curves. In this work, we present observations and analysis of the Type IIP SN 2020bij, characterized by a slow rise to its plateau as well as high expansion velocities. We identify four other SNe IIP from the literature (ASASSN-14kg, SN 2018fif, SN 2021yja and SN 2023axu) with similarly slowly rising light curves and find that they also show high expansion velocities. Using both analytical and numerical models, all five events can be explained with weak to no CSM interaction. We therefore propose that these events constitute a new subclass of Type IIP SNe which could be associated with relatively confined CSM. Early and dense photometric coverage of future SNe IIP together with early spectroscopic observations will further map this subclass and its physical properties. Understanding such rare events could be key to constraining the diversity of late-stage mass-loss in RSGs.

AI.tldr: SN 2020bij and four similar SNe IIP exhibit slow rises to plateau and high expansion velocities, forming a new subclass explained by weak to no CSM interaction, potentially linked to confined CSM from RSGs.
AI.motivation: To understand how Type II supernova explosion properties relate to progenitor properties, and to explain the rapid rise to plateau seen in many SNe IIP that requires CSM interaction.
AI.method: Observations and analysis of SN 2020bij; identification of four similar slowly-rising SNe IIP from literature (ASASSN-14kg, SN 2018fif, SN 2021yja, SN 2023axu); analytical and numerical modeling.
AI.result: The five events all show slow rises and high expansion velocities, and are explained by weak to no CSM interaction, constituting a proposed new subclass of Type IIP SNe.
AI.conclusion: These rare events may be linked to relatively confined CSM, and early dense photometric/spectroscopic coverage of future SNe IIP is needed to further characterize this subclass and constrain late-stage mass-loss diversity in RSGs.

title: Indicatives of Early Stages of Star Formation in the Universe
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, published in Astrofizicheskii Byulleten
summary: The paper analyzes formation conditions for globular clusters (GCs) in circumgalactic clouds. The similarity between the metallicity distributions of GCs in the nearby Universe and of circumgalactic clouds is substantiated in detail over a wide range of redshifts: from \mbox{0.2} to \mbox{5.9}. The distributions of the number of circumgalactic clouds and GCs both contain a sequence of four local maxima at the metallicity values: \mbox{$[\rm{X/H}]\simeq -2.6, -2.0, -1.4,-0.5$}. The sequential enrichment of a circumgalactic cloud with a mass of $10^{8}\,M_{\odot}$ is calculated starting the extremely low metallicity \mbox{$ [\rm{X/H}] <-2.3$}, then following through the stages of \mbox{$-2.3 \le [\rm{X/H}]<-1.7$} and \mbox{$-1.7 \le [\rm{X/H}] < -0.9$} to the high metallicity \mbox{$[\rm{X/H}] \ge -0.9$}, where the boundaries of these ranges coincide with the local minima of the number of objects in the distributions. It is shown that for the reproduction of such distributions, it is sufficient that at each stage of enrichment of a part of a cloud in metals, one or more GCs with a total mass of \mbox{$3 \times 10^{6}\,M_{\odot}$} are formed. It is shown that the maximum mass of stars capable of leading to supernova explosions increases with the increase of metallicity. Possible values of this mass are calculated for the metallicities corresponding to the maxima in the distributions of clouds and GCs.

AI.tldr: The paper links globular cluster (GC) formation to circumgalactic cloud enrichment across redshifts 0.2–5.9, showing matching metallicity distributions with four peaks at [X/H] ≈ -2.6, -2.0, -1.4, -0.5. It models sequential enrichment of a 10⁸ M☉ cloud and shows that forming GCs of total mass 3×10⁶ M☉ at each stage reproduces the observed distributions. The maximum mass of supernova progenitor stars increases with metallicity.
AI.motivation: To establish a quantitative connection between globular cluster formation and the metallicity evolution of circumgalactic clouds, explaining the observed multi-peaked metallicity distributions of GCs across cosmic time.
AI.method: The authors compare observed metallicity distributions of GCs and circumgalactic clouds from z=0.2 to 5.9, identify common local maxima and minima, and model the sequential chemical enrichment of a 10⁸ M☉ circumgalactic cloud from extremely low to high metallicity, calculating GC mass formation and supernova progenitor mass limits at each stage.
AI.result: Four matching metallicity peaks are identified. Sequential enrichment with GC formation of total mass 3×10⁶ M☉ per metallicity stage reproduces the observed distributions. The maximum stellar mass for supernova progenitors increases with metallicity, with specific values calculated at each distribution peak.
AI.conclusion: GC formation is directly tied to the metallicity enrichment stages of circumgalactic clouds, and the IMF upper mass limit for supernovae is metallicity-dependent, matching the observed metallicity distribution features.

title: Tracing grain growth in the forming prestellar core L1506C with 3D modeling of Herschel, IRAM, and CFHT observations
comment: 21 pages, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: In the early phases of star formation, properties of prestellar cores are commonly inferred from observations of thermal dust emission and thus depend on dust properties, which must be carefully characterized. Our target, L1506C, is part of the filament L1506 in the Taurus molecular cloud. The spectral energy distributions over the whole spectral range (from 160 μm to 2 mm), built from Herschel PACS and SPIRE and IRAM-NIKA2 data, have been fitted with a modified blackbody. These data were also modelled using the 3D radiative transfer code SOC and the latest THEMIS 2 dust model using extinction observations from WIRCam at CFHT and from Spitzer as additional constraints. The MBB modeling reveals that L1506C is fragmented into two low density cores with masses smaller than their Jeans masses. The dust color temperature and the emissivity spectral index show clear anti-correlation and change in grain properties. Grains more evolved than the diffuse interstellar medium are needed to model the densest part showing that grain growth already occurs at very early stage of star formation, even before the onset of gravitational collapse.

AI.tldr: L1506C, a prestellar core in Taurus, was studied using Herschel, IRAM-NIKA2, and radiative transfer modeling. Results show fragmentation into two low-density cores, anti-correlation between temperature and spectral index, and evidence of grain growth before gravitational collapse.
AI.motivation: To characterize dust properties in prestellar cores, as inferred dust emission properties are key to understanding early star formation but depend heavily on poorly constrained dust grain models.
AI.method: SED fitting with modified blackbody (MBB) from 160 μm to 2 mm using Herschel PACS/SPIRE and IRAM-NIKA2 data; additionally, 3D radiative transfer modeling with SOC and THEMIS 2 dust model including extinction constraints from WIRCam and Spitzer.
AI.result: L1506C fragments into two low-mass cores (sub-Jeans masses); dust color temperature and emissivity spectral index show a clear anti-correlation; more evolved grains than in diffuse ISM are required to model the densest regions.
AI.conclusion: Grain growth occurs at very early stages of star formation, even before gravitational collapse begins, indicating dust evolution is already underway in prestellar phases.

title: Assessing Ultra-Cool Dwarf Contamination in Photometrically Selected High-Redshift Galaxy Samples
summary: Ultra-cool dwarf stars (UCDs) are a common source of contamination in high-redshift galaxy searches as both sources are red and these early-forming galaxies can have sizes that are difficult to resolve even with space telescopes. Standard selection techniques, including photometric redshift estimation and color-color criteria, cannot fully eliminate this contamination. We develop \textbf{F}oreground \textbf{C}ontamination \textbf{E}valuator of \textbf{N}earby dwarf stars in high-\textbf{Z} photometrically selected \textbf{O}bjects (FC-ENZO), a code that predicts the number of dwarf stars misidentified as high-redshift galaxies for a given survey setup. FC-ENZO models the number of UCDs and evaluates the fraction of synthesized dwarf stars that passes user-specified selection methods. We compare two synthetic spectral energy distribution libraries and find that the ELF OWL library, which relaxes the assumption of chemical equilibrium, predicts larger contaminant fractions than the BOBCAT library, because of stronger absorption features around $ 1 $ \micron. The contamination fraction increases with metallicity and also depends on the adopted stellar number-density model. The dominant contaminants are T to early Y-type UCDs, which are most commonly misclassified as galaxies at $z \sim 8$. Comparing deep surveys from different space telescopes, we find similar overall contamination levels within the same redshift range. However, the contamination is concentrated near the limiting magnitude of each survey. At brighter magnitudes, the relative contamination is highest for HST (COSMOS), followed by Roman deep-tier survey, and JWST. Although the predicted contaminant numbers remain sensitive to model assumptions, FC-ENZO provides a practical tool for survey design and for identifying optimal fields for spectroscopic follow-up.

AI.tldr: FC-ENZO is a code that predicts contamination of ultra-cool dwarf stars (UCDs) in high-redshift galaxy surveys by modeling UCD populations and evaluating how many pass standard selection criteria, finding that contamination depends on metallicity, stellar number density, and survey depth, with T/Y-type UCDs being the dominant contaminants at z~8.
AI.motivation: Ultra-cool dwarf stars (UCDs) are a common source of contamination in high-redshift galaxy searches because both appear red and can have unresolved sizes, and standard selection techniques (photometric redshifts, color-color criteria) cannot fully eliminate this contamination.
AI.method: FC-ENCO models the number of UCDs using synthetic spectral energy distribution libraries (ELF OWL and BOBCAT), evaluates which synthesized dwarf stars pass user-specified selection methods, and compares contamination fractions across different stellar number-density models and survey setups (HST, Roman, JWST).
AI.result: ELF OWL predicts larger contaminant fractions than BOBCAT due to stronger ~1 μm absorption features; contamination increases with metallicity; dominant contaminants are T to early Y-type UCDs misclassified as galaxies at z~8; overall contamination levels are similar across deep surveys but concentrated near the limiting magnitude, with HST (COSMOS) having highest relative contamination at brighter magnitudes, followed by Roman deep-tier survey and JWST.
AI.conclusion: FC-ENZO provides a practical tool for survey design and identifying optimal fields for spectroscopic follow-up, though predicted contaminant numbers remain sensitive to model assumptions.

title: The Road to Identifying the Earliest Radio-Powerful AGN with the SKA
